topic.name: The Chain Rule With Logarithmic Functions

question.explanation:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ f = \ln u, \qquad u = 3x+1. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{u},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = 3. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

\[ \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x}&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}u}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{u} \cdot 3\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3x+1}\cdot 3\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{3x+1}. } \]

example.title: Differentiating a Natural Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $f(x)=\ln(4-2x)$ at the point $(1,\ln 2).$
question.explanation:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ f = \ln u, \qquad u = 4-2x. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{u},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = -2. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

\[ \eqalign{ \require{cancel} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x}&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}u}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{u} \cdot (-2)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4-2x}\cdot (-2)\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{2}{4-2x}\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{\cancel{2}}{\cancel{2}\cdot (2-x)}\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{2-x} } \]

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=1$ is \[ \eqalign{ \left.\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x}\right|_{x=1} &=\left.-\dfrac{1}{2-x}\right|_{x=1}=-\dfrac{1}{2-1}=-1 \,. } \]

Hence, the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,\ln 2)$ is $m=-1.$ Now, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

\begin{align} y-y_1&=m(x-x_1)\\[5pt] y-\ln {2}&=-1(x-1)\\[5pt] y&=-x+1 +\ln{2} \end{align}

example.title: Differentiating a Natural Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =\log(4x+6)$ at the point $(1,1).$
question.explanation:
First, we need to find the slope of the tangent line. The slope is equal to the derivative of the curve at the given point:

\[ m = \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigg|_{x=1} \]

To compute $\dfrac{\text dy}{\text dx},$ we first express $y$ as the composite function

\[ y = \log(u), \qquad u = 4x+6. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{u\ln(10)}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 4. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\[ \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}u}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{u \ln(10)} \cdot 4\\[5pt] % &=\dfrac{1}{(4x+6)\ln(10)} \cdot 4\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{4}{(4x+6)\ln(10)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2}{(2x+3)\ln(10)} . } \]

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=1$ is

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ m &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigg|_{x=1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{(2x+3)\ln(10)}\Bigg|_{x=1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{(2(1)+3)\ln(10)}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{5\ln(10)}. } \end{eqnarray}

Now we know that the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,1)$ is $m=\dfrac{2}{5\ln(10)}.$ Finally, we find the equation of the tangent line at that point:

\begin{align*} y-y_1&=m(x-x_1)\\[5pt] y-1&=\dfrac{2}{5\ln(10)}(x-1)\\[5pt] y&=\dfrac{2x}{5\ln(10)}-\dfrac{2}{5\ln{10}} + 1. \end{align*}
